arguments.heading: What happened at the argument
paragraphs: Mr. Gant argued Section 2(b) is unconstitutional. He cited separation-of-powers jurisprudence. He stated Congress directed courts to dismiss a pending case.
Ms. O'Connell noted the United States took title in 2009. She stated tribal operations faced uncertainty since then.
Mr. Shah addressed Justice Alito’s question. He sought an administrable line in separation-of-powers cases. He suggested Congress could not single out one suit in the text.

sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: This case tests the limits of congressional power over federal courts. The dispute centers on whether a statute can dismiss a specific, pending lawsuit. the sides that brought the case argue this violates separation of powers. the opposing sides argue Congress controls federal court jurisdiction.

sections.heading: What the justices asked
paragraphs: Justice Kennedy asked if the result would change without Section 2(b).

Justice Kagan asked if removing five specific words would change the outcome. She also questioned the distinction between jurisdiction and substantive law. She asked if the statute merely stripped jurisdiction. Justice Alito asked for a clear separation-of-powers rule for such statutes.

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: This case defines the boundary between legislative and judicial power. It determines whether Congress can target specific lawsuits for dismissal. The outcome shapes the independence of federal courts. It affects the stability of property rights and tribal operations. It clarifies the scope of congressional jurisdiction-stripping authority.
